title: Distributed Constraint Optimization via Online Learning and Iterative Pricing with Application to Large-Scale Satellite Scheduling

images.desc:
6.1 Graph coloring


Graph coloring is a common benchmark for distributed constraint optimization.
We evaluate all algorithms against graph coloring instances on two network topologies: random graphs and scalefree networks.
Random graphs independently construct an edge between each node in the graph with probability pp.
Scalefree networks model real-world graph structures by iteratively adding vertices to mm existing vertices with probability proportional to their degree.
We generate a test set for each graph structure with n∈{10,20,30,50,100}n\in\{10,20,30,50,100\} number of nodes for a 33-coloring problem. For each value of nn, we generate 6 random (two for each choice of p∈{4n,5n,6n}p\in\{\frac{4}{n},\frac{5}{n},\frac{6}{n}\}) and 6 scalefree networks (two for each of m∈{2,3,4}m\in\{2,3,4\}), for a total of 60 sample problems.
We run each algorithm for 10 trials on all instances.
Each algorithm runs until convergence or until 30 seconds have elapsed.
We tune hyperparameters for each algorithm by conducting a grid search over relevant values.
We provide more details in Section E.2, and a list of hyperparameters used in Table A1.


Figure 1: Cost of solution found over time for graph coloring problems across all network types.


We report the costs of mid-run solutions found by each algorithm throughout the experiment, and plot these values across time (Figure 1).
Since the network size nn vastly changes the scale of the solution costs, we first rescale the costs so that the experiments with a particular nn value have a mean value of 1.
We use gaussian kernel smoothing to plot each curve, and display the standard error as a shaded region around each curve.
We show a breakdown of the performance by network type in Figure A12.
We also report the performance by network size in Figure A13.


We found that across network types and sizes, online learning algorithms performed as well or better than existing incomplete DCOP algorithms, barring DSA.
Most online learning variants performed comparably, including RM+, Damped DRM+, IR-PRM+, and FTRL.
The damped variants of the algorithms underperformed compared to their standard counterparts, indicating that damping is not an effective technique with the RM variants.
Overall, these results support that online learning algorithms are viable for DCOPs.

6.2 Decentralized satellite scheduling


We simulate a low-Earth orbit Walker constellation composed of 60 satellites.
The constellation has 8 orbital planes at an 88°88^{\degree} inclination each containing 66 satellites. There is an overlay of 2 planes at a 51.6°51.6^{\degree} inclination containing 6 satellites each.
This configuration is motivated by the SkySat constellation [Planet, 2023], and is designed to match the number of spacecraft in the NASA FAME mission [Chien et al., 2025a].
All satellites are homogeneous; they have a memory capacity of 125 GB and a sensor that can slew to 45°45^{\degree} off-nadir.
 Figure 2 visualizes the constellation.


Figure 2: The 60-satellite Walker constellation.


We also simulate two downlink stations: the ASF Near Space Network Satellite Tracking Ground
Station and the Guam Remote Ground Terminal System.
A downlink is modeled by a bit stream of 62.5 MB/s.


For each simulation, we randomly select a horizon of six hours within a one week interval. Six hours corresponds to roughly four full orbits of Earth per satellite. We generate a request set composed of repeat observations of a random subset of 634634 of the most populous, globally distributed cities.
For each ground target, we add a request to observe it in the first half, second half, or both halves of the horizon.


Figure 3: Average quality of satellite scheduling solution found. Standard error of the sample mean is displayed.


We generate 20 problem instances (observation campaigns) for evaluation, and run each algorithm within each framework for 20 trials on each instance.
We report the utility of the final solution achieved by each algorithm in Figure 3.
We use the context-based variants of the RM algorithms, as this resulted in the best performance when paired with the iterative pricing framework.
Context-based variants had the opposite effect under constraint generation, so we display the standard variant of IR-PRM as a representative.
We provide more details on the context-based results in Section E.2.
We run each algorithm for 25 iterations, which we found to be enough for convergence (Section E.4).
The iterative pricing step size, α\alpha, is also a tunable parameter, and we show these results in Section E.3.
With each algorithm, we report the optimal α\alpha found in the iterative pricing framework.
We provide the final list of hyperparameters used in Table A2.


The best algorithm within the iterative pricing framework was context-based IR-PRM, which fulfilled 99.2% of requests.
The constraint generation framework with MGM2, fulfilled only 86.7% of the observation requests.
The iterative pricing framework performed significantly better than constraint generation with all algorithms apart from DSA-C and Maxsum-ADVP.
This difference is likely due to the combinatorial infeasibility of restricting enough schedules to force the algorithm to converge to a better solution.
Within the iterative pricing framework, all online learning algorithms performed well, fulfilling over 90% of requests.
The other incomplete DCOP algorithms failed to reach 90% request completion.
The online learning variants performed substantially better within our framework.


Finally, we compare our frameworks to NSS (Table 1).
We report the highest satisfaction variant of each algorithm, and use NSS with the GND(2) heuristic.
Our iterative pricing approach was near-optimal and satisfied over 99%99\% of requests.
NSS and the constraint generation framework only achieved around 87%87\% satisfaction.
However, NSS, which focuses on scalability, reduced the message volume substantially.
This indicates a natural tradeoff between our method and NSS: for closer-to-optimal solutions, one should select our iterative pricing framework, and for applications in which very low message volume is important, NSS is more appropriate.

E.1.1 RM Damping


When comparing different levels of damping in the RM algorithm, we find that using no damping performs the best (Figure A1).


Figure A1: Cost of solution found over time for different levels of damping in RM.

E.1.2 RM Inertia


When comparing different levels of inertia in the RM algorithm, we find that using no inertia performs the best (Figure A2).
Combined with the previous result, this indicates that when paired with online algorithms, the increased stability of damping and inertia algorithm variants comes with a loss in performance.


Figure A2: Cost of solution found over time for different levels of inertia in RM.

E.1.3 DRM α\alpha and β\beta



When comparing different values for α\alpha and β\beta in the DRM algorithm, we find there is no major difference in performance (Figure A3).
In our main experiments, we use α=1.5\alpha=1.5, β=0\beta=0 since these values are often used.


Figure A3: Cost of solution found over time for different α\alpha and β\beta values in DRM.

E.1.4 DSA


When comparing different variants of DSA (as well as different pp parameters), we find that DSA-C with p=0.3p=0.3 or p=0.5p=0.5 perform best (Figure A4).


Figure A4: Cost of solution found over time for different pp values in DSA, across different variants.

E.1.5 FTRL


When comparing different values for η\eta in the FTRL algorithm, we find there is no major difference in performance (Figure A5).
In our main experiments, we use η=1\eta=1 since this value is often used.


Figure A5: Cost of solution found over time for different η\eta values in FTRL.

E.1.6 Maxsum Damping


When comparing different levels of damping in the Maxsum algorithm, we find that using a damping parameter of 0.80.8 performs the best (Figure A6).


Figure A6: Cost of solution found over time for different levels of damping in Maxsum.

E.1.7 Maxsum Stability


When comparing different levels of stability in the Maxsum algorithm, we find that using a stability parameter of 0.010.01 performs the best (Figure A7).


Figure A7: Cost of solution found over time for different stability values in Maxsum.
